results.title: Differential Item Functioning (DIF): Complete Guide to Test Fairness | Cogn-IQ
results.content: # Differential Item Functioning (DIF). Differential Item Functioning (DIF) occurs when test items perform differently for subgroups of equal ability, potentially indicating test bias. DIF analysis identifies items that unfairly advantage or disadvantage specific demographic groups, ensuring test fairness and validity across diverse populations. Differential Item Functioning (DIF) is a statistical property of test items that occurs when individuals from different groups (such as gender, ethnicity, or language background) with the same underlying ability level have different probabilities of answering an item correctly. DIF provides a framework for identifying and addressing such bias at the item level, distinguishing it from legitimate group differences in the construct being measured. * Understand the distinction between DIF and item bias. * Learn major statistical methods for DIF detection. * Recognize the implications of DIF for test validity and fairness. Uniform DIF occurs when the performance difference between groups remains constant across all ability levels. For example, if an item consistently favors one group by the same amount regardless of ability level, it exhibits uniform DIF. Non-uniform DIF occurs when the performance difference between groups varies across ability levels. This method can detect both uniform and non-uniform DIF through hierarchical model comparison. IRT-based DIF detection compares item parameters across groups, examining differences in difficulty, discrimination, and guessing parameters. This approach addresses the contamination problem where DIF items affect the matching variable, providing more accurate detection especially when multiple items exhibit DIF. When examining DIF across multiple groups simultaneously, methods include generalized Mantel-Haenszel statistics, multiple indicator multiple cause (MIMIC) models, and multi-group IRT approaches. Bundle DIF examines differential functioning at the testlet or subscale level rather than individual items. Bundle DIF can reveal systematic bias patterns that individual item analysis might miss. DIF analysis informs item writing and revision processes. Items flagged for DIF undergo content review to identify potential sources of bias, such as culturally specific references, gendered language, or differential curricular exposure. DIF analysis provides empirical evidence for test fairness, supporting legal defensibility under employment and educational testing guidelines. In international testing programs, DIF analysis identifies items that function differently across countries or languages. A handbook on the theory and methods of differential item functioning (DIF).

results.title: The Impact of Education on Depression Assessment: Differential Item Functioning Analysis - PMC
results.content: For example, the Mini-Mental State Exam was found to include significant DIF by education for 4–5 items, which led to overestimation of cognitive errors for individuals with a lower level of education (Crane et al., 2006; Jones & Gallo, 2002; Murden, McRae, Kaner, & Bucknam, 1991; Ramirez, Teresi, Holmes, Gurland, & Lantigua, 2006). We hypothesized that DIF would be observed across levels of educational attainment for complex items on legacy measures of depression: the Beck Depression Inventory II (BDI-II), the Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale (CES-D), and the Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-9). To our knowledge, this is the first study to investigate the broad impact of educational attainment on the PHQ-9, CES-D, BDI-II, and PROMIS Depression items using DIF analysis. This study investigates the effect of education on four separate measures of depression – three questionnaires commonly used to assess depressive symptoms in the clinical setting, as well as items measuring depression from subsets of the NIH Patient Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS) item bank. DIF analysis is a method used to statistically quantify whether group membership (e.g., level of education) affects the relationship that a questionnaire item has with the construct it measures (e.g., depression). Of the measures administered in the NIH Toolbox sample, PROMIS Depression had one item with DIF, two items on the PHQ-9 were flagged, and one item on the CES-D (item 17; “*I had crying spells*”) demonstrated DIF with the largest effect size of items flagged in this sample (*R**2* = .017). In the Toolbox Calibration sample, the ICCs for PROMIS Depression Item 46 (EDDEP46) and PHQ-9 items 5 and 8 showed that individuals with the highest level of education (college graduate or above) had steeper item slopes than the other two education groups, and thresholds varied. In contrast, the ICCs for the items flagged for DIF in the PROMIS 1 Wave 1 sample, with the exception of PROMIS Depression Item 9 (EDDEP9) and CES-D Item 2, showed that individuals with the lowest level of education had the steepest item slopes. Given that DIF was found across all measures and that there is wide variability within levels of education, health literacy may have a stronger influence on IRT parameters than education for items measuring depression (e.g., Paasche-Orlow & Wolf, 2007; Taple et al., 2019).

results.title: Understanding the IRS DIF Score: How It Affects Your Tax Return
results.content: Understanding the IRS DIF Score: How It Affects Your Tax Return. Understanding the IRS DIF Score: What It Means for Your Taxes. Although it is sometimes random, the IRS generally uses a computer-generated score, called the IRS DIF score, before deciding whether to audit you. This score helps the IRS identify which tax returns may have errors or appear suspicious. However, understanding this score can help you avoid mistakes to ensure the safety of your tax return. What is the IRS DIF Score? It’s a number generated by the IRS computer screening system to assess the likelihood that a tax return contains errors or underreported income. The IRS risk assessment score from DIF doesn’t directly indicate you’ll be audited, but a high number increases the likelihood. How does the IRS DIF Score Works? The IRS DIF score system uses statistical formulae and data models to identify tax returns that appear unusual. This is how the IRS uses the IRS risk assessment score to determine if your return is risky. All these are considered IRS tax return red flags that can affect your score. How the IRS Uses the DIF Score for Audits? The IRS audit selection process depends heavily on the IRS DIF score. When the IRS receives your tax return, it undergoes a machine review. How to Reduce Your IRS DIF Score and Lower Audit Risk? If your IRS DIF score triggers an audit, remain calm. The IRS DIF score plays a significant role in determining whether your return may be audited. Can I check my IRS DIF score? A high IRS DIF score means your return stands out for review, not an automatic audit. How does the IRS verify DIF score accuracy? The IRS tests the IRS DIF score system through a special audit sample called the Taxpayer Compliance Measurement Program. How can tax professionals help with DIF score concerns? A licensed tax professional can spot issues that may raise your IRS DIF score. * What is the IRS DIF Score? * How does the IRS DIF Score Works? * How the IRS Uses the DIF Score for Audits? * How to Reduce Your IRS DIF Score and Lower Audit Risk?

results.title: How Taxpayers Are Selected for Audit Using DIF Scores
results.content: Published Time: 2025-01-18T02:56:38+00:00 How Taxpayers Are Selected for Audit Using DIF Scores – The TaxPro Blog How Taxpayers Are Selected for Audit Using DIF Scores The IRS uses a computer scoring system called the Discriminant Inventory Function (DIF) to evaluate tax returns for potential audit. The DIF score is based on a mathematical model that compares a taxpayer’s return to statistical norms derived from IRS data. Returns with unusually high or low DIF scores—indicating potential errors, misstatements, or fraud—are flagged for further review. The IRS also utilizes the Unreported Income DIF (UIDIF), which specifically targets cases of potential unreported income. However, not all flagged returns result in an audit; the IRS manually reviews many flagged returns before initiating further action. How the IRS Uses NAICS Codes to Assign Classes to Businesses Businesses are required to report their North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) code on tax returns. This six-digit code identifies the industry in which the business operates. The IRS uses NAICS codes to classify businesses into industry groups, allowing it to compare reported income and expenses with averages for similar businesses. This comparison helps identify returns that deviate significantly from industry norms, which may indicate potential inaccuracies or misstatements. For example, a business in the restaurant industry reporting unusually low food expenses relative to revenue may raise a red flag for further review. The use of NAICS codes ensures that businesses are compared to similar operations, making the audit selection process more precise. The Role of the Statistics of Income Bulletin and Averages for Line Items The IRS relies on its Statistics of Income (SOI) Bulletin and other data sets to establish averages and norms for specific line items, such as income, deductions, and credits, by income level, industry, and filing status. These statistics are derived from tax returns filed in prior years and provide benchmarks for what is typical for taxpayers with similar characteristics. When a taxpayer’s reported amounts on specific line items, such as charitable deductions or business expenses, fall significantly outside these benchmarks relative to their income or adjusted gross income (AGI), it may indicate a potential misstatement. •Disproportionate business expenses for a small business compared to industry averages may trigger further scrutiny.

results.title: The hitchhiker’s guide to differential item functioning (DIF)
results.content: Fortunately, such tools exist, one of them being differential item functioning (DIF) analysis. Pioneered by the Educational Testing Service in the 1980s (Zieky, 2011), DIF allows researchers to determine whether score differences between groups on a given test item stems from true differences in ability on the construct that the item is intended to measure (e.g. verbal reasoning ability), or construct-irrelevant differences (e.g., cultural, historical, or scientific knowledge on an item intending to measure verbal reasoning). Instead, DIF compares performance on a test item between a reference (majority) group and a focal (marginalized) group, while controlling for performance on the test as a whole (an estimate of the true difference in the construct-relevant ability) (Holland and Wainer, 1993; Zumbo, 1999). DIF analysis has been successfully used to detect problematic items in large-scale assessments such as the SAT (Sehmitt and Dorans, 1990; Zenisky et al., 2003) and it has been advocated for use in the development and testing of high-stakes assessments (Martinková et al., 2017). As of March 2021, our research team at Altus Assessments began applying DIF analysis to our situational judgement test Casper. While Casper shows smaller demographic differences as compared to scores for other commonly used admissions criteria, such as MCAT or GPA (Juster et al., 2019), we applied DIF analysis to continue our team’s pursuit of reducing demographic differences on our assessments (Casper Demographic Differences 2019-2020, 2020). Our team applied DIF analysis to 168 unique Casper test sittings that occurred between 2018–2021, containing over 2,000 test items. DIF analysis is but one approach that the testing industry should use to minimize demographic differences on high-stakes educational assessments. (2021) put it “rather than simply claim they follow established statistical procedures to screen items for differential item functioning (DIF), testing companies should commit to invest in exploring new ways of testing to effectively reduce performance gaps”.
